title: AWS identity: accounts, roles, and the caller you actually are
outcome: Set up a training identity and distinguish human sign-in, workload roles, trust, and permissions.
benefits: Explicit identity and smaller permission scope.
drawbacks: Several policy layers can affect the final decision.
version: AWS SDK for Ruby v3 · service-specific setup · no cloud resources created automatically
cue: Who calls? What action? Which resource? Under which context?

trace.title: Training account
trace.detail: An AWS request is made by a principal under a permission context. Human sign-in and application identity should be separate. Use a dedicated training account/profile and temporary credentials. A workload normally receives a role instead of a permanent access key baked into its image.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Human signs in → temporary credentials identify a principal → workload assumes its permitted role → SDK signs a request → AWS evaluates action/resource/context → result or denial. For an AccessDenied, record the caller ARN, action, resource, and request ID without secrets.

For ECS, distinguish the task role used by app code from the execution role used for platform tasks such as image/secret retrieval. In EKS, use the supported pod identity mechanism rather than giving every pod the node’s broad privileges.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail: A correct region with the wrong account can still target the wrong resource. Administrator access can make a lab pass while hiding the permission you actually need.
